title: Lab Statistics: Reference Intervals and Method Comparison
summary: Define a reference interval as the central 95%, choose nonparametric or transformed parametric estimates for skewed data, verify a borrowed interval with 20 local samples, and judge method comparisons by bias and agreement rather than correlation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 10 Hits 1, 5 (method-comparison regression) and 8, and Traps 1, 4 and 5 (first lesson for Ch. 10). Checked against Ozarda 2016 (summarizing CLSI/IFCC C28-A3) and Giavarina 2015; the original C28-A3 was not read. Nuance: the reviewer recommends Deming regression; the worked example uses Passing–Bablok regression. Not taught as fact: the reviewer’s ALT and Method C figures, Gaussian percentages, p-value/power conventions, error types, test selection, Bonferroni, r² definition, CV/SDI, geometric mean, detection limits, chi-square/Fisher rules, paired tests, CI formula.

objectives: Define a reference interval and choose between parametric and nonparametric estimation.
Apply the 20-sample rule to verify a transferred reference interval.
Explain why correlation does not show agreement and interpret slope, intercept and Bland–Altman bias.

scenes.title: r = 0.996 — can we switch?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario built on a published worked example (Giavarina 2015): a laboratory compares a new analyzer (method B) with the current one (method A). Correlation r = 0.996. The supervisor says: “Practically perfect — switch on Monday, and just copy the reference interval from the package insert.” Question token: “Does a high r prove the methods agree, and can the interval be copied?”

cues.text: A lab compares a new analyzer with its current one. The correlation coefficient is 0.996.
The supervisor wants to switch on Monday and simply copy the reference interval from the package insert.
Does a high correlation prove the methods agree? And can the interval just be copied?

props.label: High r = agreement? Copy the interval?

scenes.title: What a reference interval is
scenes.altText: Definition card (Ozarda 2016, summarizing CLSI/IFCC C28-A3): the reference interval (RI) runs from the 2.5th percentile (lower limit) to the 97.5th percentile (upper limit) of results from a reference population — the central 95%. Methods: NONPARAMETRIC estimation does not assume any distribution and is recommended by C28-A3; PARAMETRIC estimation requires Gaussian data, either directly or after a transformation (e.g. logarithmic) that is then tested for Gaussian fit. Sample size: at least 120 reference subjects (per partition) are recommended to calculate the confidence intervals of the limits. Schematic: a histogram with the central 95% shaded.

cues.text: A reference interval is the central 95 percent of results from healthy reference people: from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile.
The recommended way to find those limits is nonparametric: simply rank the results and read off the percentiles, with no assumption about their shape.
Parametric methods, such as mean plus or minus about two standard deviations, need Gaussian data, either as collected or after a transformation such as taking logarithms.
To estimate the limits with confidence intervals, the guideline recommends at least 120 reference subjects for each group.

scenes.title: Skewed data, and borrowing an interval
scenes.altText: Skew card (Ozarda 2016): when reference values are not Gaussian, a parametric estimate requires a suitable transformation tested for Gaussian fit — otherwise use the nonparametric percentiles; applying a Gaussian formula to skewed data misplaces the limits (schematic: a long right tail pulls the mean up and a ±2 SD lower limit can fall below the observed values). Transference card (Ozarda 2016, citing C28-A3): if a laboratory wants to use an RI from elsewhere (a manufacturer or another lab with a comparable method), it may VERIFY it by testing 20 reference individuals from its own population: if no more than 2 of the 20 (10%) fall outside the RI, it may be adopted, at least provisionally; if more than 2 fall outside, test a second 20; if that also fails, establish or re-evaluate the RI.

cues.text: Many analytes are skewed, with a long tail of high values. A Gaussian formula on such data misplaces the limits, and the lower limit can even fall below any value actually seen.
So skewed data need either a transformation that makes them Gaussian, or the nonparametric percentile method.
A laboratory need not always build its own interval. To borrow one, it tests 20 healthy local reference people.
If no more than 2 of the 20 fall outside, the interval can be adopted, at least provisionally. If more fall outside, test 20 more, and if that fails too, the interval must be re-evaluated.

scenes.title: Correlation is not agreement
scenes.altText: Worked example (Giavarina 2015, hypothetical data): methods A and B have r = 0.996 (95% CI 0.991–0.998), yet Passing–Bablok regression gives slope 1.06 (95% CI 1.02–1.09) and intercept 7.08 (95% CI −0.30 to 19.84): the slope CI EXCLUDES 1 → a proportional difference; the intercept CI includes 0 → no demonstrated constant difference. The Bland–Altman mean difference is −27.17 units: on average B reads 27.17 units HIGHER than A. Principle cards: correlation studies the relationship between variables, not their differences; a high r can simply reflect samples spread over a wide range; the Bland–Altman limits of agreement contain 95% of differences, but whether they are ACCEPTABLE must be defined a priori from clinical, biological or analytical goals. Hook answers: r alone does not prove agreement; verify the borrowed RI with 20 local samples.

cues.text: In a published worked example, two methods had a correlation of 0.996. But the regression slope was 1.06, with a confidence interval from 1.02 to 1.09, which does not include 1.
So method B reads proportionally higher. The Bland–Altman plot agrees: on average, B measured about 27 units more than A.
Correlation shows that two methods rise and fall together, not that they give the same numbers. A wide range of samples alone can push r close to 1.
Decide in advance how big a difference is clinically acceptable, then check the limits of agreement against it. And verify the borrowed interval with 20 local samples before using it.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “r = 0.99, so the methods agree” (✓ correlation ≠ agreement — check slope/intercept CIs and Bland–Altman bias against a priori limits); “Use mean ± 2 SD for any reference interval” (✓ only for Gaussian data — otherwise transform or use nonparametric percentiles); “The package-insert reference interval can be used as is” (✓ verify with 20 local reference individuals; ≤ 2 outside to adopt).

cues.text: Trap one: r is 0.99, so the methods agree. No: correlation is not agreement. Check the slope and intercept confidence intervals and the Bland–Altman bias.
Trap two: mean plus or minus two standard deviations works for any reference interval. No: only for Gaussian data. Otherwise transform or use percentiles.
Trap three: use the package-insert interval as it is. No: verify it with 20 local reference people first.

scenes.title: Dancing together, standing apart
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Correlation means two dancers MOVE TOGETHER; agreement means they STAND IN THE SAME PLACE. And a borrowed suit must be TRIED ON (20 fittings) before you wear it.” Tokens: r = move together · slope 1 & intercept 0 = same place · 20-sample fitting. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: correlation means two dancers move together; agreement means they stand in the same place. And a borrowed reference interval is like a borrowed suit: try it on twenty times before you wear it.

Where it breaks: even good agreement needs acceptance limits chosen in advance; the choice of regression method matters, and the worked example used Passing–Bablok; and reference intervals must be partitioned where age or sex really change results.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Reference interval = central 95% (2.5th–97.5th percentile) · nonparametric recommended · ≥ 120 per partition · verify a borrowed RI with 20 (≤ 2 outside)”, “Method comparison: r ≠ agreement · check slope/intercept CIs + Bland–Altman bias vs a priori limits”.

cues.text: A reference interval is the central 95 percent of a reference population, best estimated nonparametrically and verified locally with 20 samples, and a method comparison is judged by bias and agreement against predefined limits, not by a high correlation coefficient.

props.label: r ≠ agreement · slope/intercept CIs · Bland–Altman vs a priori limits

explanation.what: Plain language: a “normal range” is the middle 95 percent of healthy people’s results, and you should check a borrowed range on your own population; when comparing two machines, the question is not whether their results rise together but whether they give the same numbers. Scientific terms: reference interval, reference population, percentile, parametric vs nonparametric estimation, Gaussian distribution, transformation, partition, transference/verification, method comparison, correlation coefficient, regression slope and intercept, Passing–Bablok, Bland–Altman plot, bias, limits of agreement.
explanation.why: Percentiles describe the observed distribution without assuming its shape; Gaussian formulas misplace limits when data are skewed. Correlation measures association, which can be high even with a large constant or proportional bias, especially across a wide range of values; agreement must be judged on the differences.
explanation.measure: RI = 2.5th–97.5th percentile; nonparametric recommended; ≥ 120 subjects per partition; verify a borrowed RI with 20 (≤ 2 outside → adopt; else second 20) (Ozarda 2016). Method comparison: regression with CIs (slope CI excluding 1 = proportional bias; intercept CI excluding 0 = constant bias) and Bland–Altman mean difference and limits of agreement judged against a priori limits (Giavarina 2015).
explanation.differs: Nonparametric (no distribution assumed) vs parametric (Gaussian/transformed); establishing (≥ 120) vs verifying (20) an RI; correlation (association) vs agreement (differences).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: define an RI, recognize misuse of mean ± 2 SD on skewed data, apply the 20-sample verification rule, and spot bias despite a high r.

questions.stem: A laboratory adopts a manufacturer’s reference interval and tests 20 healthy local reference individuals. Three results fall outside the interval. What should it do next?

options.text: Test a second set of 20 reference individuals
options.rationale: Correct. More than 2 of 20 outside → test another 20; if that also fails, re-evaluate the RI.
Incorrect. Adoption requires no more than 2 of 20 outside.
Incorrect. Arbitrary widening is not a verification method.

options.text: Switch to mean ± 2 SD of the 20 results
options.rationale: Incorrect. 20 results are far too few to establish an interval.

questions.stem: Two methods have r = 0.996, regression slope 1.06 (95% CI 1.02–1.09) and intercept 7.08 (95% CI −0.30 to 19.84). What is the best interpretation?

options.text: A proportional difference exists (slope CI excludes 1); no constant difference is shown (intercept CI includes 0)
options.rationale: Correct. High r does not exclude bias; read the CIs.

options.text: The methods agree because r is close to 1
options.rationale: Incorrect. Correlation measures association, not agreement.

options.text: A constant bias of 7.08 is proven

options.rationale: Incorrect. r = 0.996 shows a strong relationship.

questions.stem: Reference values for an analyte are strongly right-skewed. Which approach is appropriate for the reference interval?

options.text: Nonparametric 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, or a transformation shown to give Gaussian data
options.rationale: Correct. Parametric formulas need Gaussian data.

options.text: Mean ± 2 SD of the raw values
options.rationale: Incorrect. This misplaces limits for skewed data.

options.text: Use the highest and lowest observed values
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the range, not the central 95%.
Incorrect. Not a recognized RI method.
